en: The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, Fascicle One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on Mount Khararika, in the ancient past.
The abode of the celestial immortals was filled with a great assembly of all bhikṣus; they were beyond measure, all being great śramaṇas whose outflows were entirely exhausted.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, together with immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya numbers of great beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, until the World-Honored One had finished bestowing the prediction upon Guṇakārandavatī.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent, and the great assembly did likewise.

Then, from the west, there suddenly appeared a mani-jewel known as the "Responsive Pearl" (yìngzhū), surrounded on all sides by hundreds of thousands of Śakra-devānām-indra jewels; at that moment, the Responsive Pearl stood foremost before them all.

Once the pearl had appeared, all the various colored lights belonging to that mountain vanished; likewise, the light of the gods, humans, great divine kings, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, earth, fire, wind, and water was entirely eclipsed, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata’s radiance, which did not cease.

At that time, the great assembly beheld the light of the Tathāgata—immeasurable, boundless, unspeakably unspeakable—which pervaded the ten directions like empty space; yet the light of the World-Honored One was uniquely majestic, radiant, brilliant, most wondrous, and most supreme.

At that time, all the sentient beings gathered in that great assembly each saw that their own radiance, as well as all their various sublime colors, were obscured and no longer appeared; the same was true for their physical forms, sensations, and other such phenomena.

Every place observed appears like empty space; it further obscures the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, as well as all forms of earth, water, fire, and wind, and all varieties of light. It does not confront the eyes; the ears do not hear sounds, the nose does not smell fragrances, the tongue does not perceive tastes, and the mind-consciousness and its associates cannot take it as an object. Furthermore, there is neither "self" nor "other," nor are there the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Whatever great beings sought and whatever directions they wished to observe, they could see nothing at all in those directions; they saw only the body of the Buddha, its radiance and marks of excellence, manifesting as preeminently venerable.
From afar he saw that jewel, surrounded on all sides by immeasurable and innumerable Śakras, the Indras, wearing exquisite jewels upon their persons; yet that supreme maṇi stood alone before him.

At that time, among the great assembly, only those bodhisattvas who dwelt on the ten stages, or those who had attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, or those who were in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), saw this auspicious sign and were neither startled, nor terrified, nor despondent, nor regretful.

Why is this so? Because those bodhisattvas have realized the true principle in all phenomena, clearly understood their ultimate nature, and diligently entered the gate of emptiness; for this reason, they are not startled, not terrified, and do not fall into regret or despondency.

The remaining bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, kumbhāṇḍas, and all those gathered—including pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, and non-humans—all became utterly terrified, fearful, and overwhelmed. Unable to discern this shore or the other shore, they sought one another out with hearts full of alarm, yet remained unmanifest; harboring doubts, they each thought to themselves:
"What kind of phenomenon is this?"
"What is the cause of this?
By whose power does this occur?
Desiring to resolve his own doubts, he found no one to ask.
At that time, within that ocean-like assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Brahmadaṇḍa. He rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"The characteristics of all phenomena Are truly such that no one knows them.
If a person dwells within the aggregates, The six sense faculties are all obstructed."
Observing that the single aggregate is not real—namely, this aggregate of form—they harbor doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma and delude sentient beings alike.
Excellent, Great World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the true Dharma for us.
The Tathāgata, having reached this shore and the other shore, teaches the gateway of the patient acceptance of emptiness.
Those of great diligence attain a concentration-body difficult to describe;
they wear upon their heads the supreme maṇi-jewel as an ornament.
The Celestial Lord wears a jewel upon his body, surrounded by immeasurable attendants;
because they wish to come, they first manifest these auspicious signs.
Those Bodhisattvas have all attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Those who possess such wisdom, desiring to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, have come here;
they shall preach the profound Dharma without doubt.
May the Buddha comfort this assembly; he will surely take pity upon you.
"Because these ones wish to come, they first manifest this realm.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed those bodhisattvas, saying:
"It is exactly as you have said; this is the sphere of samādhi."
If a person hears of non-abiding, that person can abide in wisdom.
This is the realm of the power of the Samādhi of Space-Pregnancy;
having attained abiding in the ineffable place, the preliminary signs of this samādhi appear.
Those who abide in these two views are perpetually deluded;
by being stained with attachment to annihilationism and eternalism, they lose both this shore and the other.
For those who hold these two views, if they desire swift liberation, [they must abandon them].
"Do not speak of these things; you shall swiftly realize the various stages.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he addressed those bodhisattvas, saying:

"Virtuous ones, although that is so, for the sake of instructing those bodhisattvas who are beginners, one should teach them the characteristics of speech. By means of skillful power, one should also teach them to take the six pāramitās as their object of focus, and even to teach them the successive arising of the fundamental characteristics of the great [dharmas], so that they may be led to realization."
Once this has been realized and known, one is thereafter able to remain without words or speech regarding all phenomena (*dharma*).

It should be understood that the place of origin of the fundamental substance must extinguish its objects of perception (*ālambana*); one should realize and know that the aggregates (*skandha*) have no inherent substance, so as not to allow others to fall into the views of nihilism or eternalism.

Having abandoned the two extremes, one is neither terrified, nor submerged, nor regretful; one does not give rise to thoughts of conceptual clinging toward any phenomena, swiftly attains the fulfillment and perfect accomplishment of all the pāramitās, and likewise does not dwell in the two views of annihilationism or eternalism.

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking this Dharma, the great assembly gathered there was able to see one another again just as before, without any difference; the various forms and radiant lights they saw were as they had been previously, and the sounds they heard were restored to their former state; what they realized and what they touched were likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One raised his right hand and proclaimed these words:
“This is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, who has come to my presence;
he has attained samādhis as vast as the waters of the great ocean, and he has fully perfected the bodhisattva practices like Mount Sumeru. In the Great...
In wisdom, he is like space; in the diligent practice of vigor, he is like a great wind;
among all forms of patience, he is like a diamond; in *prajñā*, he is like space; among the assembly of bodhisattvas, he is like a great banner;
on the path toward *nirvāṇa*, he is like a great caravan leader; and regarding all roots of goodness, he is like the earth-treasury.
For the masses of the poor, they are like a vessel of merit; for sentient beings in darkness, they are like the light of the sun;
for those who have lost their way, they are like the full moon; for those who are terrified, they are like Mount Sumeru;
for sentient beings afflicted by the diseases of the various afflictions, they are like the medicine of nectar; and for all sentient beings who have severed their roots of goodness, they are like...
The staff is like a bridge upon the path to rebirth in heaven and the road to Nirvāṇa; it is like a great ship for crossing to the other shore;
it is like a gallery for ascending to the heavens; it acts as a parasol for those who are slandered or afflicted by others;
it is like a lion among the various non-Buddhist sects; and [it provides relief] from all afflictions and fevers.
It is like cool water; it is like armor against the enemy of Māra; it is like a wise teacher for those who have erred in their training;
it is like the great earth for all roots of goodness; it is like fragrant flowers for those who delight in garlands;
it is like a clear mirror for those who maintain the precepts and know contentment; and it is [a remedy] for those who lack shame and dread of blame.
To people he is like a sword; among sentient beings afflicted by illness he is like a skilled physician;
to hungry beings he is like Śrī-devī; to thirsty beings he is like a moon-gem;
to those who are weary he is like a couch; and to those who diligently seek samādhi he is like a sun-gem.
To sentient beings who are directed toward the path to enlightenment, it is like a vehicle; to sentient beings who delight in meditative concentration, it is like a cool pond;
and to sentient beings who rejoice in the aids to enlightenment on the path to bodhi, it is like a garland of flowers.
Furthermore, for those who practice the various pāramitās, that son of good family is like a great fruit;
for those cultivating the various stages (bhūmis), he is like a mani-jewel manifesting according to need.
If a person cultivates the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they are like the pārijātaka tree;
that son of good family is like a sharp sword, for he cuts through all fetters of views.

That son of good family is like a vajra, for he destroys all habitual tendencies and afflictions; he is able to subdue all hosts of Māras, and toward sentient beings through skillful means, he is like one who understands the Earth Store (Kṣitigarbha).
That son of good family manifests supreme wisdom and skillful means.

That son of good family is able to sustain the true essence of all phenomena; furthermore, he acts as a floral garland for all pratyekabuddhas, and he is like a protective garment for the entire assembly of śrāvakas.

To all the devas, he is like pure eyes; to all human beings, he is like a direct path; to all animals, he can provide refuge; out of compassion for the hungry ghosts, he uproots the suffering of the hells.
Furthermore, toward all sentient beings, he is a great vessel of jewels and a field of merit; toward the bodhisattvas, he is like a great chariot.
That son of good family is like a great minister, who is able to constantly guard the gates of the Dharma for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the three periods of time.

That son of good family adorns his body with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and is fully endowed with the wisdom of all Buddhas; he is worthy of receiving the offerings of all sentient beings, who honor him with various kinds of ritual implements, except for the Tathāgata himself.

"You all in this assembly must go forth to welcome him, carrying various offerings and providing for him according to your strength and capacity. You should honor and praise him with various jewels, banners, canopies, incense, flowers, precious standards, flower garlands, powdered incense, ointments, and various ornaments such as necklaces. You should set out jeweled vessels filled with fragrant water to sprinkle the road clean, adorn the sides of the path with various necklaces, and sing praises and hymns in diverse ways."
"Why is this? Because all of you shall before long attain such various vessels of merit.

At that time, the entire assembly rose from their seats, turned toward the west—the direction from which the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja had come—and with heads bowed and palms joined, they paid homage from afar. Their hearts were filled with immeasurable joy and exultation; smiling with serene delight, they stood upright and composed.

Among that great assembly, the most excellent bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the great śramaṇas, kings of devas, kings of nāgas, kings of yakṣas, kings of asuras, kings of garuḍas, kings of kiṃnaras, kings of mahoragas, and the rishis possessing the five supernatural powers, each reflected:
"By what offerings shall we provide the most supreme and most magnificent ornaments and requisites to honor and serve this noble son?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja manifested his supernatural powers, transforming this trichiliocosm so that it became as level as the palm of a hand and composed of the seven precious jewels. He eliminated all mountains, rivers, saline wastelands, high peaks, rocky cliffs, hills, mounds, pits, hollows, clods of earth, gravel, foul places, filth, thorns, and pebbles, leaving nothing behind. He also removed all clouds, mists, dust, smoke, and other impurities, as well as all harsh sounds, except for various kinds of music.

Within this great trichiliocosm, all the various kinds of trees were transformed into the seven treasures; from the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of these jeweled trees issued forth subtle and wondrous fragrances. Furthermore, all the various medicinal herbs growing upon the earth—whether small or large, whether possessing branches and leaves or lacking them—all became the seven treasures.

Within this Sahā world-system of a great trichiliocosm, there is no one suffering from illness who does not attain recovery; all hells, hungry ghosts, and animals have their every suffering completely extinguished.

Those sentient beings—those who were hungry received food, those who were thirsty received drink, and those who were naked received clothing—and they further obtained various exquisite necklaces and ornaments.

Thus, within this Sahā world, all sentient beings were satisfied according to their hearts' desires; their physical forms became upright and handsome, peerless and most excellent in the world, with all six sense faculties complete and their limbs full and robust. They were freed from all afflictions, their minds attained tranquil concentration, they delighted in practicing wholesome deeds, and their minds gained pure faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Thus, all the various members of this great assembly gathered here held wish-fulfilling jewels in their left and right hands.
From within these wish-fulfilling jewels, various subtle and wondrous lights issued forth, illuminating this trichiliocosm so that it was entirely filled with radiance, leaving nothing unlit.

Furthermore, those wish-fulfilling jewels emitted various subtle and wondrous sounds, raining down various jewels, various banners and canopies, various necklaces, various flowers and perfumes; they rained down various garlands, various precious vessels, and various sweet fruits. They further rained down various priceless garments and various golden threads; they rained down various nets of pearls; they rained down various *utpala* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *padma* flowers, and *kumuda* flowers; they rained down aloeswood and other fragrances; and they rained down various powdered incenses, namely, ox-head sandalwood, red sandalwood, white sandalwood, and so forth.

The path by which that bodhisattva approaches is naturally swept and sprinkled; on both sides of the road, it transforms into corridors adorned with the seven treasures, like the Sudharmā Hall of Śakra, Lord of Devas.

Within those corridors, various jade maidens spontaneously manifested, appearing like the wives and concubines of the Māra-king of the Desire Realm; they all produced five kinds of subtle and wondrous sounds, amusing themselves with one another, whether by singing or by dancing.

Having thus manifested the jeweled colonnade, he further manifested a single parasol in the space above the Buddha’s head, like that used by the Brahma King, equal in length and breadth, measuring a full hundred yojanas.

Jeweled threads formed fine gauze-like drapery with pearls hanging like dewdrops, cascading down in all directions; various other necklaces adorned it everywhere, and from within those necklaces issued forth the five musical tones.

All the grasses and trees growing upon the great earth—whether large or small, long or short, beautiful or ugly—all emit the five kinds of celestial music, such that there is not a single sentient being who does not hear it.
Having heard that voice, there was none who did not attain the stage of non-retrogression and ultimately reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the entire assembly in the gathering, seeing the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja manifest such great supernatural power and such magnificent adornment, felt immeasurable joy and exultation in their hearts. Conceiving a sense of extraordinary wonder, they further thought:
"How shall we now arrange a special seat for that son of good family before the World-Honored One?"

At that time, a lotus throne spontaneously appeared before the Buddha, with a stem of white silver, petals of purple-gold, a dais of agate, and filaments made of Brahma-maṇi jewels. It was one krośa in both length and breadth, and its petals numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
From those flowers, there spontaneously emerged all around immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of flower-seats, exactly like the previous flowers and without any difference.
Furthermore, upon that great lotus, one saw the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja manifesting naturally, seated in the full lotus posture, with a cintāmaṇi jewel adorning his head.
Upon those surrounding lotuses, there further appeared, spontaneously manifesting, immeasurable and boundless retinues of bodhisattvas sitting in the full lotus posture.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja with these verses:
“The great bodhisattvas who have previously come, Those possessed of great renown,
Having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, Have withdrawn to sit upon lotus flowers.”
"This supreme person, having arrived, manifests a great array of adornments;
without bowing at the World-Honored One’s feet, he proceeds directly to sit upon a lotus throne.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja replied to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya in verse:
"This is what the benevolent one perceives:
the true suchness (tathatā) of all Buddhas; therein no sentient beings are seen, nor is there any defilement by conceptual discrimination.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in verse:
"If you do not perceive sentient beings, you abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
why then do you manifest such adornments?
Resolve the doubts in my mind."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya in verse, saying:
"These are the various skillful means of the wise, Employed to transform all sentient beings.
Those who do not understand True Suchness (tathatā), Being ignorant and attached, abide in conceptual discrimination."
This manifestation of wisdom is for the sake of conventional truth; it does not involve the ultimate reality where all sufferings and afflictions are absent.
Desiring to bring liberation to those beings, he thus manifests such magnificent displays.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying:
"Excellent, O worthy one!
It is so, it is so, just as you have spoken."
Even if all ordinary sentient beings were to exist, those beings could never know the matters of the expedient means and liberation pertaining to the stage of a *srotāpanna*.

Even if all sentient beings were to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, those beings would still be unable to know the matters of the expedient means and liberation pertaining to the stage of a *sakṛdāgāmin*; likewise, a *sakṛdāgāmin* cannot know the expedient means of the stage of an *anāgāmin*, an *anāgāmin* cannot know the expedient means of the stage of an *arhat*, and an *arhat* cannot know the expedient means and liberation of even a single *pratyekabuddha*.

Even if all sentient beings were to attain the path of the solitary realizers (pratyekabuddhas), like rhinoceroses dwelling alone without a companion, those pratyekabuddhas would still be unable to know the skillful means, liberation, and the realm of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in order to transform sentient beings.

Even if all sentient beings were to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they would still be unable to know the skillful means, the faithful practice, the convergence with *tathatā*, the contemplation, and the establishment of a single Bodhisattva Mahāsattva of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi endowed with eloquence; they could fundamentally not know from where it arises or from where it ceases.

This virtuous son, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, having attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), has already passed through immeasurable and boundless kalpas; he has also attained unimpeded eloquence (*asaṅga-pratibhāna*) and the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, whereby he knows the mental inclinations and movements of all sentient beings.
Because of this bodhisattva, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, having seen the manifestation of great adornment and spiritual power, attain the stage of disenchantment.

This son of good family, vanishing from this place and concealing his body so as not to appear, emerges in the western direction, where he knows the mixed teachings of the three vehicles in this realm.
For this reason, he manifests the supreme wisdom of the supernatural power of the Samādhi of Boundless Space.

Having manifested this samādhi, he causes all sentient beings to conceive a sense of weary detachment; thereafter, he manifests according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and manifests his entry into the Adornment Samādhi.
Having entered samādhi, he thereby transforms and guides immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.

Good son! If this good son were to directly manifest the adornments of the realm of True Suchness and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, all the gods and humans in the world would immediately become agitated and confused; even Bodhisattvas up to the eighth stage would be bewildered and overwhelmed, let alone others.
"Good son! No one is able to know the characteristics of the manifestations of the mental activities and spheres of this great bodhisattva.

Because this good son has attained entry into such profound and subtle dharmas of merit, he possesses such immeasurable and boundless wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*). Having already entered the ocean of all Buddhas' teachings, he is free from doubt; without relying on others for awakening, he knows the skillful means himself and is fit to act as a great king for all the multitudes of sentient beings."

"Good son! This good son, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, is like a precious banner; he can manifest the path to liberation in the heavenly realms for all sentient beings, can eliminate the diseases of affliction in their minds, and can extinguish the various great poisons of suffering within their bodies."
"Good son!

If there are sentient beings who have fallen into the wilderness of false views, beset by calamities and delusions such that they do not understand skillful means, yet desire to seek rebirth in the heavens or seek nirvāṇa."

If those sentient beings can, with a sincere heart, burn aloeswood incense and prostrate themselves in reverence at the feet of that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, this son of good family, knowing the true faith and the mental activities of those beings, perceives that although those beings have given rise to afflictions, views, delusions, and perversions, they have planted various roots of goodness in accordance with their past mental karma—whether by planting roots of goodness before the Buddhas, or before the Dharma, or before the Saṅgha; or by performing acts of giving, or acts of maintaining the precepts, or by desiring to realize the Dharma within their own minds. According to their respective capacities, he knows these things.
Whether in dreams or during the day, this son of good family appears before them and, through skillful means, reveals the path of ultimate truth.

Having employed these means, he causes all sentient beings to understand their various false views and give rise to virtuous vows; he cuts off all wrong paths, extinguishes all heterodox ways, and leads them to return to right view, so that they may truly attain those three authentic practices.
One immediately attains one's true and profound aspirations, or else encounters a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
By means of such a spiritual friend, one completely succeeds in severing the diseases of afflictions and false views that arise from the foul-smelling abodes.

Furthermore, they obtain the vow for the swift liberation from the evil realms; they immediately attain the causal conditions for excellent conduct and supreme vows; they swiftly achieve mastery over the mind and its activities, and also dwell securely within the ten profound patiences (*kṣānti*).

If there are sentient beings who are afflicted by various diseases arising within their own bodies, or those who have lost their original minds, or have lost their eyes, or have lost their tongues—those whose six sense faculties are incomplete—or those whose physical members are slightly impaired, if such sentient beings can with a sincere heart prostrate to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha or recite his name, they shall all attain their wishes.

If there are sentient beings who wish to cure an illness, they should bathe with fragrant water at dawn; having purified their body, speech, and face, they should face directly east, burn aloeswood incense, and prostrate themselves at the feet of the Great Virtuous Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha.

Furthermore, that son of good family may, within the dream of sleep, manifest before the sick person—appearing suddenly in the form of a brahmin, or Śakra, Lord of the Devas, or Śrī-devī, or Mahāprajñā-devī, or a kṣatriya, or a great minister, or a judge, or a physician, or a father, or a mother, or a boy, or a girl—and by these skillful means cause that illness to be swiftly cured.
Or again, he may manifest the skillful means of excellent medicine to cause all the ailments of those sick persons to be completely cured.
If there are sentient beings who seek material wealth, or seek extensive learning through reciting and studying sūtras and śāstras,
or who delight in tranquility and profound meditative concentration, or seek great wisdom, or seek renown, or seek artistic skills— [he manifests accordingly].
Some seek ascetic practices; some seek official rank; some seek physical beauty; some seek wealth and treasures; some seek roots of goodness;
some seek a melodious voice; some seek many sons; some seek wives and concubines;
some seek a retinue; some seek a large following; some seek the practice of giving; and some seek the observance of precepts.
Some seek patience; some seek diligence; some seek meditative concentration; some seek wisdom (*prajñā*);
some seek a beautiful voice and eloquent speech; some seek to serve others and act in accordance with their wishes;
some seek liberation from all transgressions; and some seek to exhort others to practice generosity, up to and including the practice of wisdom.

Or they may seek long life. There may be sentient beings who lack material wealth and are constantly characterized by stinginess and greed; for their sake, one desires to cause them to abandon stinginess and greed and practice giving. Or, for those who break the precepts, one desires to cause them to uphold the precepts; for those who are indolent, one desires to cause them to be diligent; and even for those who lack wisdom, one desires to cause them to study wisdom.

If there are sentient beings who have not yet attained the vehicle of meditative concentration and practice the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to liberate themselves alone, he teaches them the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, this good son manifests skillful means for those sentient beings, causing them to understand the superior practice.
If there are sentient beings who lack a heart of compassion, protecting only themselves and not rescuing others from suffering;
or if there are sentient beings who think:
"By what means shall I now act so that if any sentient being wishes to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment, I may create obstacles for them"?

Those sentient beings, wishing to turn back that mind and desiring to employ such skillful means and manifestations, instruct those sentient beings to abide in the four brahma-vihāras, and even teach them to practice great loving-kindness and great compassion.

Those sentient beings should pay homage to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja; whether dwelling in an araṇya or in a secluded place, they should burn aloeswood incense, or tagara incense, or sandalwood incense.

Having bathed with fragrant water so that body and mouth are pure, kneeling on one knee with palms joined, prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they should pay homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions and recite this mantra:
"Tadyathā | Amṛte amṛte | Karuṇike | Jvala jvala | Vījvala | Śānti-karaṇe | Karuṇike | He..."
Ramo-ra-kha-ro-ma-ra-pi-ga-ta-ri-ma-ma-kha-pu-ja-ma-na-ka-lau-ni-ka-chen-ta-ma-ni-pu-ra-ya-ka-lau-ka-sa-ba-sha-mi-sa-tha-pa-ya-a-sha-ya-to-li.
