Dharisatavibhigaṇe | 21. Karuṇikaporṇaya-dumadume | 22. Sakasaye | 23. Āśaye | 24. Sarvapaḥ ||
“Dasha, twenty-five; aśukagati, twenty-six; svāhā, twenty-seven.
When this mantra is recited, that son of good family will immediately appear before one, either in human form, or in the form of a wild beast, or in the form of a bird.

Or, although they may come and remain hidden without manifesting their forms, they observe the depth of the karmic merit of those sentient beings; according to the bodies they receive, they may emit sounds and manifest the skillful means of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), enabling those beings through a single expedient to transform immeasurable hundreds of thousands of others. They cause those who have not yet settled in a definitive vehicle to settle in a definitive vehicle—whether it be the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

In a single moment, those sentient beings, by means of the skillful application of wisdom and with little effort, are led to enter the stage of non-retrogression in the Mahāyāna; they are further instructed in various samādhis, dhāraṇīs, the perfection of patience, and so forth, until they are established within the tenth bodhisattva stage of practice.
"Good son!
This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has attained such skillful means, great compassion, and wisdom.
Good son!"
I shall now explain this to you in brief.

Suppose there were someone who could measure the void and exhaust its limits; yet the skillful means, great wisdom, great kindness, great compassion, dhāraṇīs, and samādhis of this son of good family are difficult to measure.
This Great Bodhisattva has attained such inconceivable dharmas of merit as these. Good son!

When this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha sees sentient beings who have abandoned flattery and crookedness, who are far removed from deviant minds, who have generated a sincere and profound intention and accomplished right view, who do not disparage others nor praise themselves, who have abandoned stinginess and envy and are free from flattery, and who seek neither fame nor reputation but possess pure faith—the good son takes pity upon those pure sentient beings and manifests skillful means, wisdom, and diligence. Through such skillful means, such wisdom, and such diligence, they are delivered from calamities and hardships, they resolve to attain Bodhicitta, and they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

He instructs those sentient beings to dedicate all their roots of goodness toward Bodhi, so that they may attain the true path and the stage of non-retrogression, swiftly reaching Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By practicing such skillful means, wisdom, and diligence, one will fully accomplish the six pāramitās; having developed a mind of great power, one shall swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son!
This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has attained such inconceivable, extraordinary skillful means and superior wisdom to teach and transform sentient beings."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does this good man wear a cintāmaṇi upon his head, which displays such radiance and such majestic power?”
"No other bodhisattvas possess such qualities.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son!"

This son of good family, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, has perfected great compassion for the sake of all sentient beings; he constantly transforms sentient beings without ceasing, and seeing them in great calamity and distress, he never rests in his desire to uproot their suffering.

If there are sentient beings who have committed the four grave prohibitions and are about to fall into the evil realms—having abandoned all roots of goodness and caused their manifold virtues to scatter and perish—this son of good family acts as a great physician for those sentient beings.

Seeing those sentient beings fallen into ignorance, caught in the net of false views, and imprisoned within the dungeon of peril and distress, this good man acts for their sake like the light of the sun, illuminating them so that their transgressions are extinguished and their four grave karmas are eliminated; he plucks out the thorns of doubt from the hearts of those sentient beings.

If there are sentient beings who have destroyed the vessel of their minds, and this son of good family sees those beings whose practice of the Dharma has been ruined by the encroachment of afflictions, who have lost the true Dharma and are about to enter the evil realms, who have no refuge and no protection, and who have abandoned all wisdom.

This son of good family acts as a staff for those sinful beings, manifesting the right path; he washes away their stains of sin, afflictions, and impurities until they are fragrant and pure, teaching them to turn their backs on evil paths, like a great chariot that leads them toward the celestial realms and swiftly attains nirvāṇa.
If there are sentient beings whose minds are oppressed by desire, bewildered and tormented;

if there are sentient beings for whom anger blazes intensely as they contend with one another, their pride and envy never ceasing for a moment, and who, distracted by afflictions, have lost their original mind;

if there are sentient beings shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, lacking the resolve for liberation, failing to recognize the existence of causes, and fearing nothing of the future world; [may they all attain peace].
There are sentient beings who amass vast wealth and treasures with no sense of satiety;
there are sentient beings who commit the ten unwholesome deeds without ever ceasing.

For their sake, this son of good family closes the gates to the evil realms and opens the path to the heavens and humans; like a wondrous chariot, he transports them upward to rebirth and establishes them upon the true path of nirvana and liberation.
For this reason, this son of good family deserves to receive offerings from all devas and humans, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the Buddha previously stated concerning the four grave offenses, what are these four?”

Yet when sentient beings commit the four grave offenses, they fall away from all virtues, sever their roots of goodness, and descend into the evil realms; they violate their original vows, are oppressed by afflictions, and become objects of hatred for both devas and humans.

"And this good man, seeing such evil sentient beings as these, extracts them from their suffering and distress and places them in a state of peace and happiness, causing them to attain full sufficiency.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Good man!"

All Kṣatriya kings have five grave evils; if a king commits these five evils, he loses the roots of goodness cultivated in the past, forgets his original vows, is shrouded by the veil of afflictions, and becomes estranged from all the joys of gods and humans, falling into the evil realms from which there is no time of escape.
"Good son!

If there is a kṣatriya king who has been consecrated by coronation, and he forcibly seizes the property of the Buddha, or seizes the property of the Saṃgha or the property of the *caitya* Saṃgha, or seizes items offered out of faith—whether seizing them himself or commanding others to seize them—this is called the first most evil and grave offense."

If there is a kṣatriya king who has received the consecration, and he slanders the True Dharma—whether it be the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or the Mahāyāna—and slandering it, he does not believe in it, nor does he cause others to practice it, but rather commands that it be hidden away; this is called the second most grievous and heavy offense.

If there is a Kṣatriya king who has received the consecration, and he causes my ordained disciples—who have shaved off their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes—whether they are observers of the precepts or not, to strip from their bodies the saffron robes and return them to lay life; and if he punishes them with offenses, whether by beating or binding, or by reviling and banishing them to various regions, or by ordering them to pay fines, or by casting them into prison, or by taking their lives, this is called the third extremely evil and grave offense.

If there should be a kṣatriya king who has received the consecration, who intentionally takes the life of his father, intentionally takes the life of his mother, or further takes the life of my disciple, an arhat; who causes a schism in the Saṃgha; or who sheds the blood of a Buddha.
Among these five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), if one commits even a single kind, or even merely conceives the initial thought [to do so], this is called the fourth most grievous and heavy offense.
If there is a consecrated Kṣatriya king who does not speak of causes and abandons the future world, practicing the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*).
Among the ten evil karmas, to extensively teach sentient beings to practice the ten unwholesome actions and establish the ten evils is called the fifth most extremely grave offense. Good son!

If there is a Kṣatriya king who has been consecrated by coronation, and he commits even one of these five evils, that Kṣatriya king shall lose all the roots of goodness cultivated in the past, causing them to be utterly extinguished. Having violated his original vows and being shrouded by the veil of afflictions, he loses the pleasures of gods and humans and subsequently falls into the evil realms, from which there will be no prospect of escape for immeasurable kalpas.
"Good son!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, for the sake of those sentient beings, takes birth in the borderlands to manifest his body. He may assume the dignified and composed deportment of śramaṇas, brahmins, and others; observing which form a sentient being requires for transformation, he skillfully manifests such bodily characteristics. In every place, before kings, he thus preaches the Dharma—the profound sūtras of the Tathāgata’s teaching on omniscience never heard before—and he explains and demonstrates the characteristics of the stages of practice, such as upholding the precepts and practicing patience."

If one knows that a consecrated Kṣatriya king, having previously committed various sins and performed unwholesome deeds, now feels remorse and shame, desires to atone for his transgressions and never dare to commit them again, abandons evil matters, and repents; and if he subsequently performs meritorious deeds, practices great giving, and establishes wholesome karma, he will be reborn in the higher realms and immediately attain liberation.
“Good son! All ministers have five grave offenses.
If a minister seizes the property of the Buddha, or seizes the property of the Saṃgha or the property of the *cātuddisa-saṃgha*, this is called the first grave offense.
If there is a minister who destroys a kingdom, a village, or a town; or destroys a settlement, a city wall, or another country, this is called the second grave offense.

If there is a high minister who slanders the True Dharma—whether it be the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the Vehicle of Omniscience—whether by slandering it himself or inciting others to do so, preventing its practice, and causing it to be obscured and not manifest, this is called the third grave offense.

If there is a minister who, out of malice toward the disciples of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, causes them disturbance and terror—whether they observe the precepts or not, whether they are diligent or not—stripping them of their saṃghāṭī robes and forcing them to return to lay life; or inflicting physical punishment, beating, binding, imprisonment, reviling, scolding, or intimidation; or compelling them to pay fines, or casting them into prison, or even taking their lives—this is called the fourth grave offense.
If there is a high minister who commits one, two, three, four, or all five of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), thus creating evil karmic actions—this is called the fifth grave offense.
"Good son!

If there is a minister who commits even one of these five grave offenses, those ministers will lose the fruits of their past karma; all the roots of goodness they have cultivated will be utterly extinguished. They will violate their original vows and lose the happiness of gods and humans, falling into the evil realms to undergo great and extreme suffering."
"Good son!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha, because those sentient beings are born in the borderlands, dwells in the borderlands to manifest his physical form;
he assumes the body of a śramaṇa with dignified and orderly deportment to preach the Dharma for them."
Furthermore, he may manifest in the form of a Brahmin with a dignified and solemn demeanor, or appear as a youth to preach the Dharma;
in every place, he manifests the signs of birth, preaching the Dharma according to the roots of goodness possessed by those beings.
He also reveals the unprecedented, profound, and wondrous sūtras and dhāraṇīs spoken by the Buddhas.

The bhikṣuṇī, with patience, comforted them on various stages and preached the Dharma; employing such skillful means, she caused the ministers and others to repent and confess their faults, giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse.
She led them to atone for those evil karmas and abandon all transgressions, instructing them to cultivate generosity, diligence, and the observance of precepts.
Thus establishing virtuous karma, they were reborn in the Upper Direction and attained the path to nirvāṇa.
“Good son! There are five matters by which a śrāvaka commits a grave offense.
What are these five?
First is killing;
second is committing sexual misconduct;
third is stealing.
Fourth is false speech;
fifth is destroying images and shedding the blood of the Buddha.
These are called the five types of grave and heavy offenses.

If any of my śrāvaka disciples should commit even one of the five transgressions, or any of the matters previously described, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja will, for their sake, take birth in those places and manifest his physical form. He may appear as a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, assuming their respective deportment and physical appearance to preach various subtle and profound meanings of the Dharma. He shall proclaim and expound all the sūtras, various dharanis, and all the stages (bhūmis) taught by the Omniscient One—those most profound and diverse gateways to the Dharma—so that they may hear them, repent of the various evils they have committed in the past, remember them without forgetting, give rise to deep shame and remorse, and confess those sins so as never to commit them again.

Having repented for their transgressions, they practiced generosity and fully engaged in ascetic disciplines with diligence and vigor; at the end of their lives, they were reborn in the higher realms and subsequently attained nirvana, whereupon they immediately resolved their minds to enter the Mahāyāna and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.

“Good son! There are eight matters by which a person of the Mahāyāna commits a grave offense. Having committed these eight heavy transgressions, they cause those beginner bodhisattvas to lose the roots of goodness planted in the past, resulting in their total destruction. They violate their original vows and become shrouded by afflictions; they are held in contempt by gods and humans, turn their backs on the Mahāyāna, and fall into evil realms. For a long period of time, they remain in the midst of afflictions, far removed from virtuous friends.”
"Good son! What are these eight?
If there are sentient beings who, due to the causes and conditions of evil deeds committed in the past, are born in impure lands."

Because those sentient beings lack many roots of goodness as their cause and condition, it is only through the influence of a spiritual friend that they are able to hear this profound and subtle Mahāyāna sūtra.
Those sentient beings have narrow and inferior minds, and they are likewise unable to plant many roots of goodness.

Although these beginner bodhisattvas have resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, upon hearing this profound sūtra on the characteristics of emptiness, they explain it to others and recite it.

Just as they have heard and just as they have recited it, they proclaim and expound it for those who are like various kinds of ignorant, mute sheep; before them, they preach the teachings of the Omniscient One and command them to read and recite.

Yet those ordinary persons possess no merit; because their ordinary minds cannot comprehend the profound meaning of the Dharma, upon hearing this teaching they give rise to a mind of terror and remorse. They immediately turn their backs on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and resolve instead to practice and study within the path of the śrāvakas.
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Volume Upper;
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
“Good son! This is called the Bodhisattva’s first commission of the first great sin.

Once this good son has committed this sin, he loses all the roots of goodness previously cultivated; he violates his original vow and is overcome by afflictions, unable to be reborn in higher realms, nor can he attain the bliss of Nirvana. His Bodhisattva practice becomes a mere empty exertion; having forgotten the bodhicitta, he will subsequently fall into the evil destinies.”
"Good son!

Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to transform sentient beings must first understand their minds and know their conduct; according to that conduct, they should subsequently preach the Dharma for them."
For example, it is like a person who wishes to enter the great ocean; they must first know the depth of that water before entering.

To speak briefly, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha manifests his birth in those lands and displays his physical form for the sake of those sentient beings, being well able to discern which among them have committed grave offenses and fear falling into the evil realms.
"Furthermore, if there is anyone who, out of fear of transgressions, hears others recite the name of that Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, or if they desire to behold that Bodhisattva."

Then, that bodhisattva, desiring to repent of his deep and heavy transgressions, bathes in fragrant water during the final watch of the night and puts on clean garments. Burning aloeswood incense and tagara incense, he places his right knee upon the ground and joins his palms facing east; with a focused mind, he should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, knowing the lightness or gravity of the transgressions and merits of those who have first resolved their minds toward the path of Bodhi, manifests his body according to their individual capacities; he may appear in the form of a Brahmin, or even as a boy or a girl, remaining present before them.

Having appeared before them, out of compassion for those who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], he contemplates the causes and conditions of the grave karmic offenses originally committed by those bodhisattvas and instructs them to repent. For their sake, he manifests profound, skillful, and subtle expedient means, preaching the essential points of the supreme Mahāyāna Dharma. He teaches them to establish the gates of samādhi, patience, various dhāraṇīs, and the stages of the path (*bhūmi*), thereby enabling them to be liberated from the causes and conditions of heavy sins leading to all evil realms, to abide on the stage of non-retrogression, and to advance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, they attain a great power like that of a vajra, achieving a firm resolve within the six *pāramitās*, and ultimately accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha may manifest his own body before sentient beings and, having manifested his body, preach the Dharma for them.

If the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has not yet manifested his body, then that beginner Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, during the latter part of the night, shall bathe with fragrant water, put on clean garments, burn aloeswood incense, and seek out the Great Being of the eastern quarter named Aruṇa, chanting aloud:
"O Benevolent Aruṇa!"
Out of your great compassion, you wish to appear and illuminate this Jambudvīpa; out of pity for me, arouse a heart of loving-kindness and compassion to protect and shelter me.
On my behalf, petition the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha to show me the skillful means, so that I may now repent all my grave offenses and attain the eye of great wisdom within the noble Mahāyāna.
Having thus made this exhortation and completed his prostrations, he returned to his own place and slept peacefully.

At that time, when the great being Aruṇa of yellow-white hue appeared in the east, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha immediately manifested his body within the dream of that sleeping person, appearing before the bodhisattva who had committed a grave offense. He taught that beginner bodhisattva of heavy transgression the great wisdom and skillful means for repenting his offense;

or else he manifested the wisdom of great skillful means, causing that bodhisattva who had first resolved upon the Way to attain the samādhi called "Never Forgetting the Bodhicitta," so that he might dwell securely within the Mahāyāna teachings and swiftly fulfill and accomplish the six pāramitās.
"Furthermore, good son!
There may be a beginner bodhisattva who, seeing another practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, goes to that person's place and says to them:
'You are unable to practice the six pāramitās of a bodhisattva, nor can you achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"You should give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; you shall then attain liberation from the afflictions.
...and so forth, as previously stated.
"Good son!"
This is called the second grave offense of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there may be a beginner bodhisattva who, upon seeing other sentient beings, speaks as follows:
"O person, do not practice the *prātimokṣa-vinaya* precepts; do not exert yourself within these teachings.

You should quickly resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and you should quickly read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras. By means of this, the three types of afflictive actions performed by you—namely those of body, speech, and mind—will become purified through these [very] evil karmas and afflictions."
...and so forth, as previously described. Noble son,
this is called the third grave offense of a bodhisattva who has newly entered the path.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There may be a bodhisattva who, seeing others, speaks to them in this way:
'You people, abandon the Śrāvaka-yāna; do not listen to it, read it, or recite it; do not explain it to others; conceal it and do not reveal it.'"

"You sons of good family, do not point toward the Śrāvaka vehicle; if you practice this Śrāvaka vehicle, you will not attain the great fruit, nor will you be able to sever the fetters of all afflictions."

"You should only speak the pure Mahāyāna sūtras; by listening to, reciting, upholding, and explaining them to others, through these causes and conditions you shall attain liberation from all evil realms, extinguish all such evil karma, and swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If that person hears such words from a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice and follows along with this conduct, both of those individuals commit a grave offense.
Good son!
This is called the fourth grave offense.

"Furthermore, son of good family, a beginner bodhisattva constantly engages in divisive speech with a discrepancy between mind and mouth; whatever Mahāyāna sūtras they read or recite, they do so for the sake of seeking fame, for the sake of gain and offerings, and for the sake of seeking respect and receiving sustenance. With such a mind, they read and recite the sūtras, explain them to others, receive and uphold them, and propagate them."
If, for the sake of others, one employs skillful means as appropriate, and having heard it from another, repeats it to others, saying:
"I am now a person of the Mahāyāna, while all others are not."
Thus they give rise to such feelings of jealousy for the sake of gain and offerings.

Or, seeing other practitioners of the Mahāyāna receive wealth, treasures, and the four types of requisites from others, they consequently develop a mind of resentment. For that reason, they spread base and evil reports about those bodhisattvas everywhere, slandering, reviling, defaming, and despising them, while praising themselves.
Out of such a mind of envy, they speak to others of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), saying:
"I have attained the superhuman state;
such a superior dharma, I have attained and I know it."
For this reason, because these people have violated their original vows, they are overcome by afflictions and turn their backs on the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Those sentient beings commit grave offenses against the Mahāyāna, and eventually, upon casting off their bodies, they fall into the evil realms.

It is like a person who, wishing to gather precious jewels, goes to the shore of a jewel island but does not enter the sea; or though he enters the sea, he destroys his own ship midway, so that the foolish man meets his end within the waters.
"Good son! It is so, it is so.
Those bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds to enter the ocean of the Mahāyāna are slandered and falsely accused by those deluded people out of envy."
For this reason, those deluded persons wreck the ship of faith; having wrecked the ship of faith, they extinguish the life-force of wisdom.
Son of good family!
Such beginner bodhisattvas, being thus foolish, ignorant, and of little learning, commit great transgressions by speaking falsely and slandering others due to the causes and conditions of jealousy.
“Good son! This is called the fifth grave offense of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
Furthermore, good son!”

In future ages, there will be beginner bodhisattvas, whether they be laypeople or those who have left the household life, who shall adorn all the profound dharma-gates of the characteristics of emptiness and the subtle sūtras with various dhāraṇīs, the stages (bhūmis), the patiences (kṣāntis), and various practices.
For the sake of those bodhisattvas of great wisdom, he undertakes the sphere of diligent seeking and ascetic practice.
Regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras, whether reading or reciting them, explaining or proclaiming them, or expounding, analyzing, and widely disseminating them for others, he says to them:
"I have naturally understood these sūtras; I have naturally realized and known them; I have naturally clarified them. It is I alone who, out of compassion for you all, expound them."
Having heard this from me, you shall contemplate it thus, recite it thus, and naturally comprehend this most profound Dharma.
By these causes and conditions, you shall come to possess knowledge and vision just as I do now.
Yet they are unwilling to say:
"I have read and recited such profound and subtle sūtras, which I shall now explain for you.
Such persons sell themselves for the sake of seeking gain and offerings from the fourfold assembly.

For this reason, before all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the three periods of time, as well as the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and all noble persons (pudgala), those deluded people commit a pārājika offense; having committed such a grave transgression, they falsely deceive all devas and humans.

Such deluded persons likewise lack the capacity for the Mahāyāna; how much less could they enter the Mahāyāna, how much less attain a superior state, and how much less could they ever achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to travel a long distance; while in a vast wilderness, being tormented by hunger and thirst, he suddenly encounters a grove of fruit trees and enters it, seeking the means of food in order to sustain his life.
Then that person suddenly encounters a great tree, abundant with flowers and fruit, perfected in fragrance and beauty; having encountered it, he obtains its flavor.
Having obtained this flavor, he climbs further up a poisonous tree and eats its poisonous fruit; having eaten it, his life comes to an end.
"Good son! It is even so;
these foolish people have now obtained a human body and encountered a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra). Relying upon that friend, they have entered the Mahāyāna."
Because those sentient beings seek gain and offerings, they delight in praising themselves and disparaging others; thus they commit such grave and heavy offenses.
Having committed these grave offenses, they will be held in contempt by all wise people and shall fall into the evil realms.
For this reason, none of the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras may draw near him.
Should any persons draw near him, such individuals will immediately oppose all the great wise sages and commit a grave transgression.
“Good son! This is called the first-practitioner bodhisattva committing the sixth great grave offense.
Furthermore, good son!”

In future ages, there may be Kṣatriya kings and others who, for the sake of Brahmin state preceptors of evil conduct, ministers of evil conduct, physicians of evil conduct, and the like—who are in truth foolish yet claim to possess great wisdom and great talent—shall grant them many honors and emoluments.
Those people practice various acts of giving and perform manifold meritorious deeds.

Because of their minor acts of generosity and their cultivation of such principles, they become arrogant and heedless, claiming for themselves that they possess the Way. They incite Kṣatriya kings to engage in mutual strife and destruction with my disciples, the śramaṇas, or they incite śramaṇas to engage in mutual conflict with Kṣatriya kings.
Those wicked people rely upon the Kṣatriya king to inflict punishments upon bhikṣus or to exact taxes and property from them.

Due to the pressure exerted by the Kṣatriya kings and their various ministers, those bhikṣus may deliver their own goods, or the property of the Saṃgha, or the property of the *cāturdisa-saṃgha*. Having delivered these various items as taxes to provide for the officials, they hand over those goods to the wicked men; and those wicked men then take these items from the bhikṣus to present to the Kṣatriya king.
Have both of them committed a grave and heavy offense?
Those kṣatriyas and wicked people have engaged in mutual strife and contention with the bhikṣus.

For these reasons, they abandon that True Dharma to establish what is not the Dharma; they grasp at what is not the Dharma and distance themselves from the True Dharma. They abandon the sūtras, the Vinaya precepts, the Upadeśas, and the Mahopadeśas as taught in the Mahāyāna; they distance themselves from compassion, the Prajñāpāramitā, skillful means, and the practices of the precepts found in other sūtras, discarding everything spoken by the Tathāgata without exception.

Desiring to disturb and confuse the bhikṣus, he falsely and arbitrarily contrives rules that contradict the Buddha’s Vinaya and establishes his own legal codes. Having established these codes, he disturbs the bhikṣus, causing them all to abandon śamatha, vipaśyanā, right practice, and right mindfulness; even those engaged in meditative concentration will give rise to anger and a disturbed mind, leading to constant strife and contention.
By these causes and conditions, they cause the bhikṣus to give rise to various afflictions and fail to attain tranquil concentration.
At that time, those bhikṣus lose the Dharma of right faith and lose the dignified conduct and ritual protocols of virtuous bhikṣus, causing them to fall into various views.

For these reasons, they cause all the bhikṣus to become indolent, preoccupied with worldly affairs, and unable to maintain the precepts; having broken the precepts or abandoned them, they can no longer rely on the rules of the śramaṇa, yet they say with their own mouths:
"I am a śramaṇa, a bhikṣu."
"Although he proclaims,
'I am one who practices the holy life,' his movements,
voice, and breath are like the sound of a conch shell; he speaks of the Dharma without relying upon the True Dharma."
These monks and their retinues, as well as the Kṣatriya king along with his ministers and subjects, increased their offerings twofold because of the goods they had delivered.

Such evil bhikṣus as these will, in the presence of laypeople, speak of the unwholesome deeds of virtuous bhikṣus dwelling in solitude, such as those in forest hermitages. Consequently, the wicked kṣatriya ministers and their retinues will give rise to unwholesome and slanderous thoughts toward the bhikṣus who are diligent in observing the precepts; they will seize all the requisites belonging to those diligent bhikṣus and, having seized them, bestow them upon the bhikṣus who recite the sūtras.
Both of those two have committed grave offenses.
Why is this? Because that bhikṣu in meditative concentration is a true field of merit.
Having observed in this way, one should cause them to cultivate their practice, ensuring that they do not become involved in monastic affairs.

These meditative bhikṣus shall attain samādhi, various dhāraṇīs, the stages of patience (kṣānti-bhūmi), and so forth; they shall become vessels of the Dharma, true fields of merit and genuine receptacles of blessings. Acting as the eyes of the world, they shall provide great illumination for that world to reveal the path of goodness. Establishing themselves upon the ground of practice within the field of afflictions, they shall teach all those sentient beings so that they may all attain liberation; having liberated them, they shall establish the path to nirvāṇa.
"Good son!
These are called the eight kinds of grave offenses of a beginner bodhisattva, which they fail to abandon through diligent effort.

Because of the power of the causes and conditions of the great grave offenses committed by that beginner bodhisattva, all the roots of goodness they previously cultivated are entirely forgotten and lost; having lost them, they fall into the evil realms."
Violating their original vows, they are overcome by afflictions and lose the bliss of gods and humans; deluded by falsehoods, they lose the bodhicitta.

Good son! For the sake of such good sons as these, this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is born in that land to manifest bodily forms for those sentient beings—sometimes appearing in the body of a bhikṣu with dignified and orderly deportment, or appearing in the body of a brāhmaṇa fully accomplished in majestic conduct, even manifesting the deportment and signs of an animal for those who are to be transformed through an animal form; in brief, it is as described in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

One should know that this case is likewise: skillfully discerning the various faculties and mental dispositions of beings, he manifests his body accordingly and teaches the Dharma to those sentient beings in a manner suited to them. He instructs them in various unprecedented teachings, universally manifesting for them the subtle and wonderful sūtras, dhāraṇīs, stages of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), and so forth, as proclaimed by the Omniscient One. He causes those beginners among bodhisattvas who have committed grave offenses to give rise to a sense of shame and remorse; causing them to feel dread and a heart of repentance, he leads them to confess those heavy sins, so that they may distance themselves from them, abandon them, and never dare to commit them again.

“Good son! If those sentient beings, out of fear caused by having committed grave offenses, hear the name of this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and desire to see his body—fearing they will fall into the evil realms and wishing to repent for their sins—those sentient beings should prostrate at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha and further invoke his name with a sincere mind.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, according to their faculties and karma, manifested his bodhisattva body-form right before them: for those who were to be delivered by the body-form of a bhikṣu, he manifested the body-form of a bhikṣu;
for those who were to be delivered by the body-form of a brāhmaṇa, he manifested the body-form of a brāhmaṇa;
and for those who were to be delivered by the body-form of a boy or a girl, he manifested the body-form of a boy or a girl.
Observing those beginner bodhisattvas according to the gravity of their transgressions, he manifests himself accordingly.

Through such skillful means, he instructs them to repent, demonstrating the practice of skillful means within the profound Dharma of the Unsurpassed Vehicle. Whether on the correct stages or the incorrect stages, whether among the various samādhis, dhāraṇīs, or patiences, he manifests and teaches their practice, even gradually instructing them to establish themselves in the station of the Eightfold Noble Path.

By the power of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, those sentient beings shall be liberated from all the sufferings of the evil realms; having been liberated from the evil realms, they shall be established in the stage of non-retrogression, and once so established, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Good son! It is so, it is so.

Those bodhisattvas, through great power and diligent application within the practice of the six pāramitās, are like flashes of lightning; they swiftly achieve the realization of the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

“Good son! If the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja does not manifest his physical form before a Bodhisattva who has committed a grave offense, that Bodhisattva who has newly committed a grave offense shall, in order to recognize his own transgression and seek to invite the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, bathe with scented water during the final watch of the night, put on clean garments, kneel on one knee with palms joined, face the east, burn aloeswood incense, and with a sincere heart entreat the yellow-white Ābhāsvara Devaputra of the eastern quarter.
One should speak thus: "Arūṇa! Arūṇa!"
You possess great compassion and great merit.

When you first emerged from the east and shone universally upon Jambudvīpa, out of your compassion, I pray that you will protect me and swiftly entreat the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, who is endowed with great pity, so that this Bodhisattva may specifically manifest skillful means for my sake while I am asleep.
"By means of skillful expedients, you have taught me to repent for the grave offenses I have committed, so that I may swiftly attain the eye of wisdom within the Great Sage’s Mahāyāna.
Having spoken these words, that Bodhisattva-practitioner of grave offenses returned to his room and lay down to sleep.

"At that time, when the yellow-white Aruṇa appears over Jambudvīpa in the east, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja immediately follows behind, manifesting in the form of a bodhisattva before the eyes of those bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice. Within their dreams, he manifests skillful means to teach those who have committed offenses how to repent of their evil karma, providing such skillful means and insights before those bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice."

Having performed these skillful means, the beginner bodhisattva immediately attains a samādhi called "Non-forgetfulness of Bodhicitta. Within the Mahāyāna, they attain a firm dwelling from which they cannot be regressed or shaken; they swiftly accomplish the six pāramitās and shall before long realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Good son! This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has exerted the greatest diligence to accomplish the most supreme task; he has perfected a sublime and wondrous *maṇi* jewel that fulfills all desires, which is uniquely manifested as it is strung upon his crown.”
“Good son!
This Bodhisattva Gaganagañja possesses such an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable accumulation of merit.
Furthermore, good son!”

If there are sentient beings who hear the name of this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, or who fashion his image and make offerings to this Bodhisattva with various ritual implements—respecting, revering, prostrating to, and praising him; and making offerings to him with various kinds of incense, flowers, garlands, unguents, powdered incense, and burning incense, as well as with various banners, canopies, and precious standards.
Having made these offerings, they further honored, revered, and paid homage to them, entrusting their own lives to those bodhisattvas.

By the power of that bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority, fire could not burn them, water could not drown them, and weapons could not wound them; they could not be harmed by anything within any land, and in all places, humans and non-humans alike were ultimately unable to steal away their vital energy, except when their life-span was exhausted.

Should they fall gravely ill, they shall not suffer long; they shall not meet their end through the pressure of hunger; they shall not be unjustly harassed by government officials; and they shall not commit grave offenses.

Until the moment when life comes to an end, the eyes do not perceive forms, the ears do not hear sounds, the nose does not smell odors, the tongue does not experience tastes, and the body does not experience tangibles; there remains only a subtle breath, the warmth within the body, and a subtle consciousness that has not yet departed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha manifests his own body for those sentient beings.

If there are sentient beings living in the world who place their faith in the Brahmins, when such a son of good family is about to depart from the body at the moment of his final consciousness, the Bodhisattva manifests before them in the form of a Brahmin to inspire joy in them.
If there are sentient beings who previously served the Mara King, when their lives later come to an end, this Bodhisattva Akāśagarbha manifests in the body of a Mara King.

Even for those in the world who take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, Maheśvara, Śakra, a Cakravartin King, the Sun or Moon deities, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, or Vaiśravaṇa, and even for various worldly mountain spirits, tree spirits, river spirits, or spirits of springs and wells—whichever such beings they may follow as their refuge—the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja manifests himself in precisely those forms. At the time of their death, he appears before those assemblies, manifesting his form in accordance with whatever heart’s wishes those beings possess, appearing before them to grant them all.
Having manifested that body, he spoke these words:
"If a person, by means of wisdom, is able to see the Four Truths,
that person will be able to cross to the other shore from within the midst of afflictions."
"Once those sentient beings have perceived and understood this Dharma through their mental consciousness, they will be reborn in favorable realms.
If there are sentient beings who should be transformed by means of a Buddha-body, he immediately manifests a Buddha-body and stands before those beings, speaking these words:
'If one reaches the depths of the Buddha’s wisdom, One can cross the ocean of afflictions.'"
"One shall swiftly realize wisdom and attain liberation from all sufferings.
At that time, because those sentient beings recollected the Buddha and heard the Buddha’s voice, their hearts were filled with joy.
After the end of their lives, they will leave the world of the five turbidities and be reborn in a pure land, where they shall encounter various Buddhas and hear and receive the True Dharma.
This applies briefly to the Dharma and the Sangha as well.
"Good son!
This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has attained such inconceivable dharmas of merit as these.
Good son!"

Furthermore, if there are persons who, within their own minds, desire to attain various samādhis and achieve great mastery, those sentient beings should rise from sleep during the final watch of the night, bathe with fragrant water, burn aloeswood incense, and according to their ability and means, offer various articles of worship to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and prostrate at his feet.
Having made offerings and paid homage, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and speak these words:
"Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, who has attained the gate of great compassion and has already acquired wisdom, quickly turn your thoughts toward me."
"Quickly remember me!
May you always grant me the skillful means of right mindfulness and samādhi.
He then recited the mantra, saying:

“‘Tad-ta-tha (1) luo-mu (2) luo-na-ji (3) bo-che-ni-lie (4) sa-mu-da-lo-duo-lie (5) duo-na-ye-na-ye (6) mo-he-jia-liu-ni-jia (7) a-nu-po-she-bo-san-wu-li-di (8) a-jia-lo-she-bo-san-wu-li-di (9) ba-zhe-luo-yen-bo-san-wu-li-di (10) hu-lu-she-san-wu-li-di (11) a-na-mo-san-wu-li-di (12) pu-duo-ju-chi-san-wu-li-di (13) Sva-hā (14). Having recited this mantra, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority, one immediately attains right mindfulness and enters the various gates of samādhi.”
Furthermore, if there is a person who wishes to recite various sūtras and śāstras— whether those spoken by the Buddhas or those spoken by the Śrāvakas— that person,

during the final watch of the night when the pale yellow light of dawn appears in the eastern quarter, shall bathe with fragrant water, put on clean garments, kneel with the right knee on the ground facing east, burn aloeswood incense, and according to their means, make offerings and prostrate to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Giving rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, he spoke these words:
"Bodhisattva Gaganagañja!
O son of noble family!"
Having already attained a boundless and inconceivable mind of compassion for all sentient beings, you have, with great wisdom, thought of me and thought of me.
You are a bodhisattva, a most excellent *pudgala*, who possesses right mindfulness, various supreme samādhis, skillful means, and profound, vast wisdom.
He then recited the mantra:
"Tad-ta (1) Nīla-sabbe (2) Kampa-sabbe (3) Jambūnada-sabbe (4) Pakṣa-same (5) Pāṭala-jasi (6) Sattana-sulave (7) Huma huma (8) Mahākālunika (9) Svāhā (10). "Good son!"

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who wish to enter the great ocean to gather various precious gems; or those whose hearts desire to enter beneath the earth into the palaces of the asuras; or those who wish to obtain the elixir of longevity that fixes one’s age; or those imprisoned, confined, and locked up in jails; or those suffering the separation from loved ones; or those encountering hateful enemies whom they cannot avoid; or those facing the perils of fire, the perils of water, the perils of blades and staves, or the perils of malevolent poisons; or those cursed by incantations; or those facing the perils of lions, tigers, and wolves; or those facing the perils of pythons, snakes, vipers, and scorpions; or those beset by thieves and bandits, or the perils of illusions and delusions, or any kind of peril involving fear.

If there are sentient beings who face the hardships of being bound by cangues, shackles, stocks, or fetters; or those seized by government officials; or those facing execution, banishment, or the severing of their life-force; or those afflicted by chronic illness, bedridden and debilitated, or oppressed by pestilence and terrified of death; or those lacking food, clothing, bedding, medicine, or essential resources.

Those sentient beings, during the latter part of the night at the time when the dawn light begins to appear, bathe with fragrant water, put on clean garments, and prostrate to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha. Kneeling on their right knees with palms joined and facing east, they offer whatever ritual implements they have prepared according to their power and means to that Bodhisattva. Generating a heart of loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings, they utter these words:
"Ākāśagarbha, endowed with great loving-kindness and compassion, you constantly act for the benefit of all sentient beings."
"Think of me, think of me!
With a heart of compassion, may you look upon my mind; may you liberate me from the hardships previously described.
One should then speak these verses:
“I possess the marks of misfortune; may you grant me merit.
I now suffer from poverty and lowliness; please fulfill my wish this very day.”
“Gaganagañja Bodhisattva is my place of refuge;
as he is in this world, may he grant me happiness in the future.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, hearing the words of those sentient beings’ voices, manifested his original bodhisattva body, or even manifested the bodies of boys or girls, and stood before them, consoling them, saying:
"Protecting against all fears and calamities, may all terrors be entirely extinguished.

Thus it is briefly stated; for those sentient beings who are impoverished and destitute, or those who lack the means to sustain their lives, one contemplates their minds and fulfills their wishes, bestowing upon them everything they require.
“Good son! If there is a prince who wishes to attain the rank of consecration or wishes to fulfill his duties,
that prince should make offerings to that great bodhisattva, invoking his name and making offerings to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja according to his power and capacity.”

Even those beings who desire to attain the rank of a *brāhmaṇa*, the rank of a wealthy elder, or the rank of a great householder; those who wish to learn various arts and crafts, to realize the inner Dharma, to obtain incantations, to study technical skills, to hear a single verse, or to aspire toward liberation—if such beings hear this name of Ākāśagarbha, then during the final watch of the night when the dawn begins to break, they shall bathe with fragrant water, put on clean garments, face east, kneel on their right knees with palms joined, and prostrate themselves before the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Having taken refuge in him, they join their palms in supplication and speak these words:
"Gaganagañja, you who possess great compassion; as I am of meager merit, grant me the signs of merit and fulfill my heart's wishes."
One should speak these verses:
"May that which my heart seeks never be lacking;
I pray you arouse a mind of compassion, And through your loving-kindness and pity, fulfill my wish."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, with his pure divine ear surpassing that of humans, having heard this sound from those sentient beings, would manifest his own body before them for the sake of those beings; he would observe the mental activities and states of mind of those beings and provide whatever was appropriate for them according to their capacity.
"In this way, and in this way, he manifests skillful means for those sentient beings.
Good son! This Bodhisattva Gaganagañja has attained such functional mastery of skillful means that he enters the great ocean of wisdom."
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha possesses such inconceivable matters as these. Good son!
If there were another person who could count every single drop in the waters of the four great oceans and know their total number;

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja possesses skillful and supreme wisdom and expedient means for teaching and transforming all sentient beings; the manifestations of his expedient means are beyond calculation or knowledge.
"Good son!
Suppose there were someone who could know the limits and the measure of the places in the empty space of the ten directions—both those where forms can be manifested and those where they cannot;
yet the number of sentient beings taught through the skillful means of this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja could never be known."

For the sake of all sentient beings, he employs skillful means, manifesting through the transformation of his own body; he may appear in the form of a Buddha to transform sentient beings, or appear in the form of a brahmin to teach and transform them, even manifesting various bodily forms as appropriate for those who are to be transformed, appearing in those very forms without any conceptual discrimination.
To those who should be transformed by means of an animal body, he manifests as an animal;
to those who should be transformed by means of a hell-being body, he manifests as a hell-being body.
There are sentient beings for whom he manifests transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) in their very presence;
there are sentient beings who should be benefited by his appearing within dreams, for whom he manifests a body within their dreams;

and there are sentient beings who, at the point of death, possess only subtle consciousness—desiring to extinguish their various sins, sever the evil realms, and lead them toward the good realms—for those beings, he transforms into various kinds of bodies.

Regarding these sentient beings, on the day they are still alive, whichever deity they have taken refuge in—such that by seeing that deity they would immediately attain peace and happiness—even unto leading them to a virtuous realm, [the Buddha] shall manifest that very deity to cause them joy.
"Good son!
For this reason, no one can know the measure of the limits of the number of the emanation bodies of this Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha. Good son!"
This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has attained such inconceivable, supreme wisdom of skillful means, and is fully endowed with these most excellent dharmas.
This Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has already entered the ocean of the merits of all Buddhas.
“Good son!
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha wears upon his head a manifest maṇi-jewel.

At that time, all the great assembly gathered in the hall, having heard from the Buddha these praises of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, conceived toward the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha a sense of rare and extraordinary wonder, and gave rise to a heart of supreme reverence and respect. They all joined their palms and remained gazing up at him, offering various kinds of incense, flowers, powdered incense, ointments, banners, canopies, precious standards, multicolored robes, various jeweled necklaces, and diverse musical performances with songs and hymns of praise, making offerings to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja took the aforementioned offerings and presented them to the World-Honored One.
Having made these offerings, he knelt with his right knee on the ground before the World-Honored One, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How can one perform the work of a Buddha within the minds of sentient beings who, in this age of five turbidities, are shrouded by the great darkness of ignorance?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
For example, space is neither bound nor liberated, neither visible nor deluded, and the essence of space is pure by its very nature.
However, within space, due to the movement of wind, dust, mist, smoke, and clouds appear; therefore, space is merely called impure.

Due to rain and water, one becomes free from those obstructing factors such as dust; consequently, the sun, moon, and constellations become manifest, whereby one comes to know the *kalā*, *lava*, seasons, the length of day and night, the half-months and full months, and the number of years and celestial cycles.
"So it is, so it is, noble son!

Just as the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena of the Tathāgata conforms to space, the fundamental characteristic and original nature of the mind are pure; it is only because sentient beings have their minds and thoughts clouded by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) that they appear turbid."

For their sake, the Tathāgata rains down the rain of compassion through such Dharma-gates as loving-kindness; thus, those sentient beings who have been defiled by afflictions immediately attain purity, free from all stains.
When those sentient beings attain purity of mind, they behold the appearance of the Buddha-sun in the world.

Once moistened by the light of wisdom, they spontaneously come to understand within themselves the inconceivable merits of all Buddhas. He establishes them in the supreme four foundations of mindfulness and the Noble Path, and even establishes them in the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), in great loving-kindness and great compassion, and in the true Dharma; for this reason, there appear in the world Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and various Bodhisattvas.
“Good son! What do you think?
Can the nature of space abide within the eye?”
He replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha asked,
"Can the eye abide within consciousness?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Does the eye abide in contact? He replied, "No."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"Regarding the three kinds of feeling produced by contact within the eye, does space abide therein?"
He replied,
"No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said:
"To speak briefly, one should likewise practice such contemplation regarding the ears, nose, tongue, and body.
Good son!..."
"What do you think?
Does the mind abide in the realm of space?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
...And does it abide within the space of the mind?"
"Does it not arise from this Dharma that the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"Do all sentient beings dwell relying upon space? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"What do you think?
Does the nature of space abide depending upon sentient beings?
After the Buddha had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Each does not abide in dependence upon another; within their own respective domains, they do not encroach upon one another.
World-Honored One!”

All dharmas have no objective sphere; because they are empty, they are undefiled, identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and identical to suchness (tathatā). One should know them in this way, World-Honored One!

It is like space: indestructible, undifferentiated, not forming distinctions, immovable and unobstructed; without sprout, without seed, without fruit; without name, without character; without thought, without recollection.
"So it is, so it is,
World-Honored One!
Having thus known the characteristics of all dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the forbearance of the non-arising of all dharmas."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī:

"Tad-ta (1) | Vāpaha-raja (2) | Manu-kṣaya (3) | Jina-jaya (4) | Jana-ni-mo (5) | Muni-hara (6) | Anaya (7) | Para-prā-phe (8) | Karava-ni-mo (9) | Anidraya (10) | Apasa-śava (11) | Śana-śamo (12) | Naśata-ta (13) | Karamo-śamo (14) | Kṛma-duvi-śamo (15) | Citataya (16) | Kiri-śadu (17) | Saṃśu-śani (18) | Svāhā (19).
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!"
“Good son!

You are able, through this *dhāraṇī* of the Eye that Subdues the Victorious Lion’s Steady Gait, Water-Snorting Roar, to eliminate the obstacles of afflictions, the obstacles of karma, and the obstacles to the Dharma at the time of death for all sentient beings, when their final exhalation is about to pass away. Having eliminated these obstacles, you cause them to be born in pure lands.”
"Good son!

You are able to travel through immeasurable and boundless worlds of the Buddhas, giving rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings. Reaching villages, towns, cities, provinces, prefectures, counties, official palaces, and various kingdoms, once you have arrived at these places, you manifest various forms and various modes of deportment, preaching the Mahāyāna sūtras to transform and teach sentient beings. In the midst of the evil conduct of kṣatriyas, and even the evil conduct of śramaṇas, you sever their various unwholesome dharmas and establish them all within wholesome dharmas."

At that time, when the World-Honored One preached this Dharma, immeasurable and boundless devas and worldlings within the great assembly attained various samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and patiences; some further attained the true wisdom within the dharmas of the ten stages.
Ten thousand beings attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the state of non-arising.

If there were sentient beings who clung to space as being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), once they had encountered this light of the lamp, their roots for conditioned giving were entirely severed, and their practice of unconditioned giving was swiftly and fully accomplished.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, among the great assembly—the bhikṣus and others, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Brahmā, Śakra, and the four world-protecting Great Kings—all who heard this wondrous sutra preached by the Buddha were filled with joy and respectfully put it into practice.
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Scroll II.
